doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Teaching tone, melody and old standards; bridging with people
summary: His tips for full sound, using old tunes like Jada, and his melodic approach that helped bridging in Blood, Sweat & Tears with Halligan and Kooper.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And I’m happy. I said — and then if they’re playing a little soft I say, “Look,” I play my horn, I said, “This is what a professional volume is.” I’m not bragging. And I fill up the room. I play soft too. I say, “Look” I start with a buzz [scats]. And I give them a couple of hints that I thought of, no one told me this. Two things to think about. Because I remember playing clarinet or alto, like it’s a little mouthpiece, when I was 14 or 15, so you’re blowing into this mouthpiece and you’re trying to do something. Think of it as the wall right over here because in the room where I teach the wall is right there. I say imagine you’re playing to the wall. Forget about the mouthpiece. You go [scats] sing it out. Or, imagine you’re on stage at Carnegie Hall or Symphony Hall, and audience or no audience, you’re playing to someone in the balcony. And just sing out the note. Don’t overblow but just sing it out and try to hear it nice and full [scats]. Any note. And they do that. So if they get the note once I say man you’ve got it. It’s up to you. That’s what you have to do. And you don’t have to play loud all the time, but if you’re playing in a sax section lead alto, you need to play full or you’re going to sound like an inner part. So that’s what I give to them. Most of them can’t improvise, that I’ve been teaching. I back them up on piano a lot and we play standard tunes. And in the last couple of years I felt, and I’ve told the students, I think I’ve been teaching wrong, jazz. The wrong approach for a long time. There’s no right or wrong approach. But now I give them some old tunes, like “Jada” or which “Doxy” is based on, I don’t know if you knew that you know. And I point it out to them. I have them play both melodies or whatever. But some of the old standard tunes, the Louis Armstrong in say 1930s, just great, beautiful melodies, and without getting into “Confirmation” and great Charlie Parker tunes, let’s start with something simple. A great melody. And I tell them too, I’m very melodic, and I think this © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

helped me with Blood, Sweat & Tears, everything in my life, who I am. Because I like to bridge to people. It’s not for the pat on the back, “Fred you sound great.” It’s because I care about people. So I always believed that Dick Halligan and myself as arrangers for Blood, Sweat & Tears and the original, not quite a leader, Al Kooper, I think we all care about bridging. And I don’t think every jazz player does care about that. So if you don’t dig it man, you know, whatever. I don’t know. I’m just into, and it’s not for someone to say, “Fred you play great.” I know I can play. It’s just to communicate. That’s the way I am. Maybe I had good parents. I don’t know.
